source_text: Omwes enim ii valde posteriores sunt quam ° Episcopi, quibus Apostoli tradiderunt Ecclesias: et hoc in tertio libro cum omni diligentia manifestavimus. Necessitatem ergo habent predicti heeretici, quoniam sint ceeci ad veritatem, alteram et alteram ambulare exorbitantes viam: et propter hoc inconsonanter et inconsequenter dispersa sunt vestigia doctrine ipsorum. Korum autem squi ab Ecclesia sunt semita, circumiens mundum universum, quippe firmam habens ab Apostolis traditionem, et videre nobis donans omnium unam et eandem esse fidem, omnibus unum et eundem Deum Patrem precipientibus, et eandem dispositionem incarnationis Filii Dei credentibus, et eandem donationem Spiritus et eadem meditantibus preecepta, et eandem figuram Sejus que est erga Ecclesiam ordinationis custodientibus, et eundem exspectantibus adventum Domini, et eandem salutem totius hominis, id est anime et corporis, sustinentibus. 2. 7Et Ecclesize quidem preedicatio vera et firma, apud quam et eadem salutis via in universo mundo ostenditur. Huie enim creditum est lumen Dei, et propter hoe sapientia Dei, per quam salvat omnes homines, in ewitu canitur, in plateis autem Jiducialiter agit, in summis muris predicatur, i tn portis autem tatis constanter loquitur. Ubique enim Ecclesia preedicat veriet heee est lérrdyvyos lucerna, Christi bajulans lumen. Qui ergo relinquunt preeconium Ecclesize imperitiam sanctorum arguunt, non contemplantes quanto pluris sit religiosus a blasphemo et impudente sophista. Tales sunt autem omnes heeretici, et qui se plus aliquid preeter veritatem invenire putant, sequentes ea que preedicta sunt, varie et formiter et imbecille facientes iter, de iisdem non semper easdem habentes, velut czci a czecis circumducuntur, juste cadent in sublatentem ignorantiz foveam, semper queerentes et nunquam verum invenientes. Fugere igitur oportet sententias ipsorum, ®et intentius observare necubi vexemur ab ipsis: confugere autem ad Ecclesiam, et in ejus sinu educari, et dominicis enutriri. Plantata est enim Ecclesia Paradisus in hoc Ab omni ergo ligno Paradisi escas manducabitis, ait Spiritus Dei, id est, ab omni Scriptura dominica manducate: super Selato autem sensu ne manducaveritis, neque tetigeritis universam heereticam dissensionem. Ipsi enim confitentur semetipsos agnitionem habere boni et mali: et super Deum qui fecit eos, jaculansensus suos impios. Supra igitur sentiunt quam est mensura sensationis. Quapropter et Apostolus ait: Non plus sapere, quam oportet sapere, sed sapere ad prudentiam ; ut non illorum manducantes agnitionem, eam que plus quam oportet sapit, projiciamur de Paradiso vite: in quem Dominus inducit eos, qui obediunt » ejus, vecapitulans in se omnia qua in coelis, et que in terra; sed quee in ccelis spiritalia sunt, quee autem in terris secunhominem est dispositio. Heee igitur in semetipsum recapitulatus est, adunans hominem spiritui, et spiritum collocans in homine, i ipse caput spiritus factus est, et spiritum dans esse hominis caput: per illum enim videmus, et audimus, et loquimur.
thought_title: The Unity of the Church's Doctrine
pass_a_gloss: For all those heretics are indeed much later than the bishops to whom the Apostles handed over the churches, and we showed this in the third book with all diligence. Therefore, the aforementioned heretics have a necessity, since they are blind to the truth, to walk in another and another way, deviating from the path, and because of this, the footprints of their doctrine are dispersed in a discordant and inconsequent manner. But those who are from the Church, walking around the whole world, have a firm tradition from the Apostles, and it gives us to see that there is one and the same faith for all, one and the same God the Father being worshipped by all, and the same disposition of the incarnation of the Son of God being believed, and the same gift of the Spirit being meditated, and the same precepts being thought, and the same figure of the ordination which is towards the Church being kept, and the same expectation of the coming of the Lord, and the same salvation of the whole man, that is, of the soul and the body, being sustained. And the Church's preaching is indeed true and firm, in which the same way of salvation is shown in the whole world. For to it has been entrusted the light of God, and because of this, the wisdom of God, through which He saves all men, is sung in the streets, acted judicially in the squares, preached on the highest walls, and constantly spoken at the gates. For the Church preaches the truth everywhere, and this is the lamp, carrying the light of Christ. Those who leave the Church's preaching, therefore, accuse the ignorance of the saints, not considering how much more valuable is the religious man than the blasphemous and impudent sophist. All heretics are such, and those who think they have found something more than the truth, following the things that have been said, making their journey in various and weak ways, not always having the same things, as if they were led by the blind, justly fall into the pit of latent ignorance, always seeking and never finding the truth. Therefore, it is necessary to flee from their opinions and to observe more intently, lest we be disturbed by them, and to flee to the Church, and to be educated in its bosom, and to be nourished by the Lord's things. For the Church has been planted as a paradise, in which from every tree of paradise you will eat, says the Spirit of God, that is, from every Lordly Scripture you will eat, but from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you will not eat, nor will you touch the whole heretical dissension. For they themselves confess that they have the knowledge of good and evil, and they throw their impious senses against God who made them, sensing more than the measure of sensation. Wherefore also the Apostle says: Do not be wise beyond what is necessary to be wise, but be wise unto sobriety, lest, eating their knowledge, which is wiser than it ought to be, we be cast out of the paradise of life, into which the Lord leads those who obey Him, recapitulating in Himself all things that are in heaven and on earth, but the things that are in heaven are spiritual, and the things that are on earth are according to the disposition of man. For He has recapitulated all things in Himself, uniting man to the Spirit, and placing the Spirit in man, He Himself has become the head of the Spirit, and gives the Spirit to be the head of man, for through Him we see, and hear, and speak.

pass_b_english: All these heretics came long after the bishops to whom the Apostles entrusted the churches, a point we proved in the third book with every care. Because they are blind to the truth, they are forced to wander off onto one divergent path after another, so the footprints of their teaching lie scattered in discordant, incoherent disarray.

But those who belong to the Church walk the whole world over, bearing a firm tradition from the Apostles that lets us see one and the same faith everywhere: one and the same God the Father worshipped by all, the same mystery of the Son's incarnation believed, the same gift of the Spirit received, the same precepts pondered, the same pattern of ordination that serves the Church preserved, the same hope of the Lord's return cherished, and the same salvation of the whole person—soul and body—upheld.

The Church's preaching is true and steadfast, and in it the single way of salvation is displayed throughout the world. To the Church has been entrusted the light of God; therefore the wisdom of God, by which He saves all people, is sung in the streets, acts with authority in the squares, is proclaimed from the highest walls, and speaks constantly at the gates. Everywhere the Church preaches the truth, and she is the lamp that carries the light of Christ.

Those who abandon the Church's preaching accuse the saints of ignorance, never weighing how far the godly person surpasses the blasphemous, shameless sophist. All heretics are of this stripe, along with those who imagine they have discovered something beyond the truth. Following the paths already laid out, they make their journey in varied, shapeless, feeble ways, never holding the same convictions twice, like blind men led by the blind. Justly they fall into the pit of hidden ignorance, always searching, never finding the truth.

We must therefore flee their opinions and keep a more intent watch, so that we are not shaken by them; we must take refuge in the Church, be reared in her bosom, and be nourished with the Lord's own food. For the Church has been planted as a paradise in this world. 'From every tree of the garden you may eat,' says the Spirit of God—that is, from every Scripture that belongs to the Lord you may eat; but from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you must not eat, nor touch the whole heretious dissent (Genesis 2:17).

The heretics themselves claim to possess the knowledge of good and evil, and they hurl their impious judgments against the God who made them, presuming to know more than the measure of perception allows. That is why the Apostle warns: 'Do not be wise beyond what it is fitting to be wise, but be wise unto sobriety' (Romans 12:3), lest by eating their knowledge—which is wiser than it ought to be—we be cast out of the paradise of life. Into that paradise the Lord leads those who obey Him, recapitulating in Himself all things in heaven and on earth. The things in heaven are spiritual; the things on earth are ordered according to man's nature.

He has recapitulated everything in Himself, joining man to the Spirit and placing the Spirit in man. He Himself became the head of the Spirit, and gives the Spirit to be the head of man, for through Him we see, and hear, and speak.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text. Pass A provides a faithful literal rendering, and Pass B provides a fluent rendering that preserves all nuances, including the distinction between the spiritual and earthly realms. Scripture citations (Genesis 2:17 and Romans 12:3) were correctly identified and added to Pass B based on the content of the Latin text.
